segments.text: Welcome to operating systems lecture five on caching.
We begin with a historical note about magnetic core memory and early DRAM latencies.
Modern CPUs are much faster than main memory access latency.
Without a cache hierarchy every load would stall the pipeline for hundreds of cycles.
A CPU cache stores frequently used data closer to the processor.
The goal is to reduce average memory latency using locality.
Temporal locality means recently accessed lines are likely reused.
Spatial locality means nearby addresses are often accessed together.
Caches are organized into sets and ways; associativity trades hit rate for lookup cost.
On a cache hit the data returns from the fast cache hierarchy.
On a cache miss the system fetches the block from slower main memory.
Misses may be classified as compulsory, capacity, or conflict misses.
Write policies include write-through and write-back with dirty bits.
Write-allocate versus no-write-allocate changes miss handling behavior.
Replacement policies such as LRU approximate recency under limited hardware budgets.
Multi-level caches L1 L2 and L3 form an inclusion or non-inclusion hierarchy.
Coherence protocols keep private caches consistent across cores.
False sharing can destroy performance even when logical data is independent.
Prefetchers try to hide latency by guessing future accesses.
Next lecture covers virtual memory and page tables.
